extracted.intended_audience: district court judges and patent litigators managing patent cases
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for structuring early case-management in patent litigation, including claim/term winnowing, timelines, use of tutorials, and the sequencing of discovery and claim construction under Federal Circuit and Supreme Court precedent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technology tutorials (submitted or recorded)
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts may require or encourage a technology tutorial to provide context about highly technical or unfamiliar terms and issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Benefits: (a) may help focus issues and force the parties to avoid extraneous material; (b) can reduce the time needed for claim construction; and (c) gives both parties an equal chance to have the last word. Recorded tutorials can be provided to new judicial clerks and can be part of the appellate record. Tutorials set the stage for argument and may be especially useful before Markman hearings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent and claim winnowing (Model Order phased limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a phased process to limit the number of asserted claims and prior art presented, reducing complexity and litigation costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model Order specifics: Not later than 40 days after the accused infringer produces documents showing operation of accused instrumentalities, plaintiff must serve a Preliminary Election of Asserted Claims asserting no more than ten claims per patent and no more than 32 total claims. Not later than 28 days after the Court issues its Claim Construction Order, plaintiff must serve a Final Election identifying no more than five asserted claims per patent (from the ten) and no more than 16 total claims. The Model Order permits relaxation when only one patent is asserted (increase per-patent limits by 50%, rounding up). Courts may allow adding claims that present unique issues as to liability or damages. Parties encouraged to discuss lower limits based on case-specific factors (commonality among patents, number/diversity of accused products, technology complexity, claim complexity, and other issues).

rubrics_metrics.name: Step-wise limitation of asserted claims across stages
rubrics_metrics.description: Limit asserted claims at multiple stages (before claim construction, after claim construction, and before trial) to allow refinement of theories as the case progresses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A step-wise approach lets plaintiffs refine theories through discovery, claim construction, and dispositive motions. Some courts impose initial limits, then further limits after claim construction and before trial; the process should allow plaintiffs opportunity to add claims presenting unique liability or damages issues and should be flexible rather than immutable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt and apply Patent Local Rules (PLRs) to structure claim-construction process
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent-specific local rules establish a standardized timeline and framework for disclosures and submissions leading up to claim construction (Markman) proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purpose: to present the court with a limited set of meaningful disputes, require early notice of infringement and invalidity contentions, counter 'shifting sands' litigation tactics, crystallize theories early, and set natural boundaries for discovery. PLRs typically require early, relatively specific contentions and may set presumptive limits (e.g., number of terms to be construed). PLRs are presumptive and judges may modify them for good cause, but modifications must be consistent with Federal Circuit case law when issues are unique to patent law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow a standardized PLR timetable for disclosures and briefing
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a structured schedule for case-management conference, asserted-claims disclosures, invalidity contentions, identification of claim terms, preliminary constructions, joint statements, discovery close, and claim-construction briefing/hearing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical Northern District of California timetable (example): (1) CMC set by court; (2) Disclosure of Asserted Claims/Infringement Contentions within 10 days of CMC; (3) Invalidity Contentions within 45 days of (2); (4) Identify Claim Terms to be Constr. within 10 days of (3); (5) Preliminary Claim Constructions within 20 days of (4); (6) Joint Claim-Construction Statement within 60 days of (3); (7) Close of Claim-Construction Discovery within 30 days of (6); opening, responsive, reply briefs and Markman hearing spaced with specified day-intervals. Courts may adapt timetable depending on complexity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt an accelerated timeline when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a streamlined schedule for less complex cases or when parties jointly agree, potentially eliminating patent-specific initial disclosures and a separate Markman hearing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example accelerated timeline (‘Track B’): produce opinion of counsel within two months after CMC; close fact and expert discovery on accelerated calendar; combine claim-construction and summary-judgment briefs and hearings within compressed intervals (e.g., 5 months after CMC for opening briefs). Decision to accelerate should follow discussion of substantive issues driving the case (technology simplicity, little dispute about structure/function of accused devices).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit number of claim terms at the Markman hearing (typically ten)
rubrics_metrics.description: Presumptively restrict the number of claim terms presented for construction at the principal Markman hearing to focus on the most significant terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many courts set a default ten-term limit (parties jointly identify ten terms likely to be most significant, including those that may be case- or claim-dispositive). Courts may require parties to explain why particular terms are significant. The limit can be increased or decreased for good cause; additional terms can be sought in later phases. The ten-term limit avoids peripheral disputes and focuses the court on key issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure claim-construction briefing and oral argument with judge-managed procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Use joint claim-construction statements, technology tutorials, focused briefing, and (where helpful) hearings combining counsel argument and, rarely, witness testimony; exercise broad judicial discretion to manage timing and process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some courts allow parties to let terms emerge in briefing; others require joint statements. The judge should consider interrelation of claim construction with discovery, summary judgment, and settlement. Courts decide whether to hold a hearing based on whether it will be helpful (e.g., divergent expert perspectives). Practices vary by district and judge; the court’s decisions should promote focused, efficient resolution of claim-meaning disputes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy of intrinsic evidence with controlled use of extrinsic evidence under Teva
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim construction should be grounded in intrinsic evidence (patent document and prosecution history); Teva allows district courts to make subsidiary factual findings based on extrinsic evidence when necessary, but intrinsic evidence prevails where it diverges from extrinsic evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teva endorses a hybrid review: subsidiary factual findings are subject to 'clearly erroneous' review while ultimate claim-construction decisions receive de novo appellate review. Where extrinsic evidence is needed, the court should: (1) delineate disputed subsidiary factual questions prior to Markman; (2) conduct focused briefing with supporting expert declarations and evidentiary hearings to create an adequate record; and (3) prepare a careful Markman order explaining the basis for the construction. Courts must exercise due caution in entertaining extrinsic evidence to avoid waste and escalate expert battles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manage expert testimony and extrinsic evidence for claim construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Early identification and careful management of expert evidence is recommended, with options to limit or structure expert proceedings to prevent unnecessary cost and delay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts should ask parties early whether they intend to rely on expert testimony and the substance thereof. If fact-finding is planned, focused expert declarations and evidentiary hearings may be used. Court may employ the 'hot tub' method (direct engagement among experts and judge) to sharpen issues and assess credibility. For non-technical/common terms, expert testimony may be less useful and can be limited or disallowed. Judges should weigh the likely benefit against potential for escalating expert battles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Phase discovery in relation to claim construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Tailor fact and expert discovery timing to the needs of claim construction: allow targeted pre-construction discovery about accused products when necessary, but limit discovery on unrelated issues until after claim construction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although claim construction is based on intrinsic evidence, knowledge of accused product structure/function and relevant prior art often informs which claim terms need construction. Many PLRs expressly provide for discovery prior to claim construction, including mandated early disclosures of infringement and invalidity contentions. Courts should discuss potential limits or phasing of pre-claim-construction discovery to avoid wasting resources on damages, willfulness, or other matters that claim construction may render unnecessary. When claim construction is conducted after fact discovery, standard written discovery can be more feasible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide post-claim-construction fact and expert discovery as warranted
rubrics_metrics.description: After a claim-construction order, permit additional fact and expert discovery to address issues implicated by the court’s constructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claim-construction orders may reveal previously uninvestigated features of accused devices; courts commonly set fact discovery to proceed for a period after construction. Inventor depositions for Markman purposes may be initially limited to claim-construction topics, with broader depositions allowed after the Markman process. Expert discovery similarly may follow claim construction to address newly implicated issues.
